'''Michael Boris Green''' {{postnominals|country=GBR|FRS|HonFInstP}} (born 22 May 1946) is a British [[physicist]] and a pioneer of [[string theory]]. He is a professor of theoretical physics in the School of Physics and Astronomy at [[Queen Mary University of London]], emeritus professor in the [[Faculty of Mathematics, University of Cambridge#Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics|Department of Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics]] and a fellow of [[Clare Hall, Cambridge]]. He was the [[Lucasian Professor of Mathematics|Lucasian professor of mathematics]] from 2009 to 2015.<ref name="times">{{Cite web|first=Mark |last=Henderson |url=http://timesonline.typepad.com/science/2009/10/stephen-hawkings-successor-as-lucasian-professor-of-mathematics-michael-green.html |title=Stephen Hawking's successor as Lucasian Professor of Mathematics: Michael Green |work=[[The Times]]|location=London |date=20 October 2009 |access-date=20 October 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100218002526/http://timesonline.typepad.com/science/2009/10/stephen-hawkings-successor-as-lucasian-professor-of-mathematics-michael-green.html |archive-date=18 February 2010 }}</ref><ref name="cam">{{Cite web|url=http://www.admin.cam.ac.uk/news/dp/2009102005|title=Michael Green elected 18th Lucasian Professor at the University of Cambridge|publisher=University of Cambridge|date=20 October 2009|access-date=20 October 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091025205245/http://www.admin.cam.ac.uk/news/dp/2009102005|archive-date=25 October 2009|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="scopus">{{Scopus|id=7406237287}}</ref><ref>{{cite web
|url=http://www.admin.cam.ac.uk/reporter/2014-15/weekly/6380/section2.shtml#heading2-7
|title=Cambridge University Reporter No 6380
|date=18 March 2015
|access-date=19 March 2015
}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Green was born the son of Genia Green and Absalom Green. He attended [[William Ellis School]] in London and [[Churchill College, Cambridge]]<ref name="whoswho" /> where he graduated with a Bachelor of Arts with [[first class honours]] in theoretical physics (1967) and a PhD in [[elementary particle|elementary]] [[particle physics|particle theory]] (1970).<ref name="mathgene"/><ref name="greenphd">{{cite thesis |degree=PhD |first=Michael Boris|last=Green |title=Crossing symmetry and duality in strong interactions|publisher=University of Cambridge |date=1970 |url=http://ulmss-newton.lib.cam.ac.uk/vwebv/holdingsInfo?bibId=8946|author-link=Michael Green (physicist)}}</ref><ref name="dirac">{{cite web|url=http://libraryold.ictp.it/FP-DB/docs/1989/Dirac-1989-Citation-Green.pdf|title=Dirac Medal 1989 Presentation Ceremony Leaflet|access-date=20 October 2009|date=April 1990|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110722035331/http://libraryold.ictp.it/FP-DB/docs/1989/Dirac-1989-Citation-Green.pdf|archive-date=22 July 2011}}</ref>

==Career==
Following his PhD, Green did [[postdoctoral research]] at [[Princeton University]] (1970–72), Cambridge and the [[University of Oxford]]. Between 1978 and 1993 he was a Lecturer and Professor at [[Queen Mary, University of London|Queen Mary College]], [[University of London]], and in July 1993 he was appointed [[John Humphrey Plummer Professor of Theoretical Physics]] at the University of Cambridge. On 19 October 2009 he was confirmed as the next [[Lucasian Professor of Mathematics]], to succeed [[Stephen Hawking]] on 1 November 2009.<ref name="times"/><ref name="cam"/> In 2015 he was succeeded in that chair by [[Michael Cates]], a specialist in colloids, gels, and particulate materials.

==Research==
After many years in collaboration with [[John Henry Schwarz]], he co-discovered [[type II string theory]] in 1982,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Green|first1=M.B.|author-link1=Michael Green (physicist)|last2=Schwarz|first2=J.H.|author-link2=John Henry Schwarz|date=1982|title=Supersymmetrical string theories|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0370269382911108|journal=Physics Letters B|volume=109|issue=6|pages=444–448|doi=10.1016/0370-2693(82)91110-8|pmid=|arxiv=|s2cid=|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and later the anomaly cancellation in type&nbsp;I string theory in 1984.<ref name="anomaly">{{Cite journal | last1 = Green | first1 = M. B. | author-link1 = Michael Green (physicist)| last2 = Schwarz | first2 = J. H. | author-link2 = John Henry Schwarz| doi = 10.1016/0370-2693(84)91565-X | title = Anomaly cancellations in supersymmetric D = 10 gauge theory and superstring theory | journal = Physics Letters B | volume = 149 | pages = 117–122 | year = 1984 | issue = 1–3 |bibcode = 1984PhLB..149..117G }}</ref> This latter insight, named the [[Green–Schwarz mechanism]], initiated the [[First Superstring Revolution]]. Green has also worked on [[Dirichlet boundary condition]]s in string theory which have led to the postulation of [[D-brane]]s<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Green | first1 = M. B. | last2 = Harvey | first2 = J. A. | last3 = Moore | first3 = G. | title = I-brane inflow and anomalous couplings on D-branes | doi = 10.1088/0264-9381/14/1/008 | journal = Classical and Quantum Gravity | volume = 14 | pages = 47–52 | year = 1997 | issue = 1 |arxiv = hep-th/9605033 |bibcode = 1997CQGra..14...47G | s2cid = 250825225 }}</ref> and [[instanton]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Green | first1 = M. B. | last2 = Gutperle | first2 = M. | doi = 10.1016/S0550-3213(97)00269-1 | title = Effects of D-instantons | journal = Nuclear Physics B | volume = 498 | pages = 195–227 | year = 1997 | issue = 1–2 |arxiv = hep-th/9701093 |bibcode = 1997NuPhB.498..195G | s2cid = 15365248 }}</ref>

==Awards and honours==
Green has been awarded the [[Dirac Medal (IOP)|Paul Dirac]] and [[Maxwell Medal and Prize|Maxwell Medals]] of the [[Institute of Physics]], UK, the [[Dirac Medal (ICTP)|Dirac Medal]] of the [[International Centre for Theoretical Physics]] (Trieste) and the [[Dannie Heineman Prize for Mathematical Physics]] of the [[American Physical Society]]. He was elected a Fellow of the [[Royal Society]] in 1989.<ref name="royal"/> Green has co-authored more than 150 research papers.<ref name="scopus"/><ref name="spires">{{Cite web|url=http://www.slac.stanford.edu/spires/find/hep/www?rawcmd=f+ea+green,+michael+b.|title=Michael Green Bibliography listing|publisher=[[SPIRES|Spires High Energy Physics]] database|location=Stanford University|access-date=22 October 2009}}{{dead link|date=January 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

His nomination for the [[Royal Society]] reads{{centred pull quote|Distinguished for his outstanding contributions to quantum field theory, especially the theory of superstrings. Green's early work was largely on duality in S-matrix theory. He was the first to prove an important result on the dual model – the cancellation of the leading divergences between boson and fermion loops. He has made significant contributions to the theory of phase transitions, but is best known for his trail-blazing work, much of it in collaboration with Schwarz, on superstring theory, including the first covariant formulation of the theory. The most important results are the proofs in 1984 and 1985 of anomaly cancellation for SO (32) and E8xE8 superstring theories and of infinity cancellation in the SO (32) case.
These definitive papers initiated the explosive growth of superstring theory, now one of the most active and exciting areas of fundamental theoretical physics.<ref name="royal">{{cite web|url=http://royalsociety.org/DServe/dserve.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqDb=Catalog&dsqCmd=show.tcl&dsqSearch=(RefNo==%27EC%2F1989%2F10%27)|title = Green, Michael Boris: Library and Archive Catalogue|publisher=[[The Royal Society]]|access-date=11 November 2013|location=London}}</ref>}}

On 12 December 2013, Michael Green shared the [[Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics]] with [[John Henry Schwarz]] "for opening new perspectives on quantum gravity and the unification of forces".

==Selected publications==
* Green, M., John H. Schwarz, and [[E. Witten]]. Superstring Theory. Vol. 1, Introduction. Cambridge Monographs on Mathematical Physics. Cambridge, UK: Cambridge University Press, 1988. {{ISBN|9780521357524}}.
* Superstring Theory. Vol. 2, Loop Amplitudes, Anomalies and Phenomenology. Cambridge, UK: Cambridge University Press, 1988. {{ISBN|9780521357531}}.
